description: Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and recycles the phosphorylated inositol species that mark membranes for identity and release calcium-mobilising second messengers. Its outputs govern how vesicles are sorted, how endosomes and autophagosomes mature, and how receptor signalling is terminated, so cells depend on it for membrane traffic as much as for signal transduction. Lipid kinases such as PIK3C2A, the class III enzyme PIK3C3 and the 5-kinase PIKFYVE phosphorylate inositol head groups on endosomal and autophagic membranes, while the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase synaptojanin removes phosphates to drive clathrin uncoating at synapses, and inositol monophosphatase completes the cycle by freeing myo-inositol for resynthesis. Loss of this turnover is damaging in neurons in particular: synaptojanin mutations cause parkinsonism and epileptic encephalopathy, and lithium acts partly by inhibiting the monophosphatase step.

A mixed immune-expression module centred on mononuclear leukocyte identity and trafficking, combining chemokine receptors, GTPase-of-immunity-associated proteins and transcriptional regulators. Monocyte and macrophage recruitment to inflamed tissue depends on CCR2 and CX3CR1, whose ligands direct patrolling and infiltrating cells to vessel walls and injured sites; loss of this axis blunts inflammatory monocyte egress from bone marrow and reshapes atherosclerotic and neuroinflammatory disease. The GIMAP proteins act in lymphocyte survival and homeostasis, linking the set to T cell persistence as well as myeloid function. Signalling and feedback components include the IL-1 receptor accessory protein required for interleukin-1 responses, the MAPK phosphatase DUSP4 that dampens kinase output, the TNF-family receptor FN14, and the immediate-early factor NR4A3. Numerous KRAB-type zinc finger proteins and the repressor HIC1 suggest accompanying transcriptional control, alongside metabolic and autophagy-related members.

Rho family GTPases switch between GDP- and GTP-bound states to control actin and myosin behaviour, and the cycling of that switch is what makes cell shape change and division possible. The genes here connect this cycle to mitosis: ECT2 acts as an activator that loads GTP onto RhoA at the equatorial cortex, while RACGAP1, its partner in the centralspindlin complex, restrains Rac and helps position that signal between the separating chromosomes. Several GTPase-activating proteins, including ARHGAP11A and ARHGAP19, return Rho proteins to the off state, so cortical contractility is confined in space and time. PRC1 bundles antiparallel midzone microtubules and CEP55 contributes to abscission, while E2F2 links the whole programme to cell cycle transcription. The pathway therefore ties Rho nucleotide cycling to furrow ingression and the completion of cytokinesis.

Progression through the mitotic cell cycle is how a cell duplicates its chromosomes and partitions them into two daughters, and the genes here mark the commitment to divide and the machinery that executes division. Mitotic cyclins pair with CDK1 to drive entry into mitosis; the activating phosphatases CDC25A and CDC25C oppose the inhibitory kinase PKMYT1, so that entry is switch-like and occurs only once replication is complete. FOXM1 sustains transcription of the mitotic programme, PLK1 coordinates spindle assembly and mitotic exit, while PLK4 and the centrosomal CEP proteins license centriole duplication so that exactly one bipolar spindle forms. Microtubule and kinetochore factors such as gamma-tubulin, CKAP5 and NEK2, together with shugoshin-mediated protection of centromeric cohesion, ensure accurate chromosome segregation. Loss of control at these steps yields aneuploidy, mitotic catastrophe or unchecked proliferation.

Cells attach to each other and to the matrix around them, and this cell adhesion programme supplies both the ligands and the receptors that make those contacts. It underlies tissue architecture, wound healing, leukocyte recruitment and platelet plug formation, and its dysregulation contributes to fibrosis, thrombosis and tumour invasion. Fibrillar and network collagens together with fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, periostin and thrombospondins build the adhesive substrate, while integrins such as the platelet fibrinogen receptor pair ITGA2B/ITGB3, the von Willebrand factor receptor complex GP1BA/GP9, and endothelial adhesion molecules VCAM1, SELP and junctional JAM3/ESAM mediate binding under flow. Chemokines CXCL12 and IL8 and the cytokine IL1B activate these receptors on circulating cells, and SNAI2 links the same machinery to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coupling adhesion to migration and matrix remodelling.

These genes outline the differentiated macrophage phenotype: the receptors, enzymes and transporters that let a tissue macrophage sense, ingest and degrade material and then shape the local immune tone. Phagocytic signalling runs through the Fc receptor gamma chain and the kinase BTK, while CYBB supplies the catalytic subunit of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase that generates microbicidal superoxide; its loss causes chronic granulomatous disease. Degradative and secreted components such as CPVL, IFI30 and cystatin C act in the lysosomal and extracellular compartments. A second arm is immunoregulatory and metabolic: IDO1, KMO and KYNU catabolise tryptophan along the kynurenine route, dampening T cell responses, and heme oxygenase 1 together with copper and amino acid transporters handles the iron, copper and arginine flux of heme turnover. MAFB is among the transcription factors associated with macrophage differentiation.

This grouping captures the transcriptional signature of mature B cells, the antibody-producing lineage of adaptive immunity, and its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted. The core is the antigen receptor complex and its immediate modulators: CD79A and CD79B transmit immunoglobulin engagement into intracellular signalling, while CD19 amplifies that signal and CD22, CD72 and BTLA restrain it, setting the threshold at which a B cell responds to antigen rather than ignoring it or reacting to self. Complement receptor CR2 links innate opsonisation to B cell activation, CXCR5 directs homing into follicles and germinal centres, and HLA-DOB tunes peptide loading for presentation to helper T cells. MS4A1, the CD20 target of depleting antibodies, and Fc receptor-like proteins complete a profile that distinguishes B cells in tissue and blood expression data.

A mixed group of broadly expressed regulators that keep housekeeping functions of the cell running: chromatin-associated and transcriptional components, RNA-binding proteins, and machinery for endosomal membrane traffic and cytoskeletal contractility. Several members act on gene expression — a chromatin-interacting subunit of a histone deacetylase-containing repressor complex, a cyclin partner of the CDK8 kinase module of Mediator, and the zinc-finger transcription factor SP3. Others control the fate of mRNAs after they are made: MBNL1 governs alternative splicing of muscle and neuronal transcripts, FMR1 represses translation at synapses and its loss causes fragile X syndrome, and G3BP2 nucleates stress granules when translation stalls. A third arm handles membranes and organelles, including the ESCRT-associated ATPase VPS4B in multivesicular body formation, a phosphoinositide phosphatase acting at the Golgi and ER, and a myosin phosphatase targeting subunit that tunes actomyosin tension.

This grouping captures the machinery and cellular context of MHC class II antigen presentation, the route by which peptides derived from internalised material are displayed to CD4 T cells to initiate and shape adaptive immune responses. The core is the HLA-DR heterodimer together with its several beta-chain loci, and the HLA-DM chaperone that catalyses removal of CLIP and edits the peptide repertoire toward stable, high-affinity ligands. Around them sit the surface and adaptor proteins of professional presenting cells and other leukocytes: ICAM1 and the beta-2 integrin chain ITGB2 provide the adhesion needed to form a stable contact with the responding T cell, while PTPRC (CD45), CD53, LAPTM5 and intracellular adaptors including AIF1, FYB and PLEK support receptor signalling and membrane trafficking in immune cells. Expression of this programme largely defines antigen-presenting and haematopoietic identity in tissue transcriptomes.

Myeloid dendritic cells that have taken up antigen in peripheral tissues must travel to draining lymph nodes to meet naive T cells, and this directed migration is what the pathway describes: movement of a myeloid dendritic cell along a chemical gradient. The core of it is a chemokine receptor and its two ligands, produced by lymphatic endothelium and stromal cells of lymphoid tissue, which guide cells into lymphatic vessels and into T cell zones. Receptor engagement is translated into polarised actin remodelling through Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange activity, giving the cell a leading edge oriented up the gradient. The myeloid transcription factor SPI1 places this behaviour in the context of dendritic cell identity and development. The pathway therefore links innate antigen capture to the initiation of adaptive immune responses, and belongs to the wider biology of leukocyte chemotaxis and lymphoid tissue organisation.

Behind every replication fork, newly synthesized DNA must be repackaged into nucleosomes, and replication-dependent chromatin assembly is the route by which that happens in step with strand elongation. Without it, daughter genomes remain abnormally accessible, replication stress and DNA damage signalling rise, and the epigenetic states that define a differentiated cell fail to be propagated through division. Newly made histone H3-H4 dimers are received by soluble chaperones such as NASP and handed to ASF1A and ASF1B, which pass them to the CAF-1 complex; its large subunit CHAF1A binds PCNA at the fork, positioning CHAF1B and the histone cargo for deposition onto nascent DNA, after which H2A-H2B completes the particle. RBBP4 serves as a shared histone-binding module in CAF-1 and related chromatin complexes, linking this assembly step to chromatin maturation and heritable gene silencing.

Sugars attached to serine, threonine, tyrosine or hydroxylysine side chains give secreted and membrane proteins their bulk, charge and binding specificity, and protein O-linked glycosylation covers all of the routes by which these chains are initiated and extended. Mucin-type synthesis begins with a large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases and the core-1 galactosyltransferase with its chaperone, then branches, sialylates and fucosylates to build selectin ligands and mucus barriers. Separate arms make O-mannose glycans on dystroglycan, whose loss causes congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye involvement; O-fucose and O-glucose on EGF repeats, which tune Notch; collagen galactosyl-hydroxylysine; and the xylose-primed linker that nucleates heparan and chondroitin sulfate chains, with sulfotransferases and epimerases setting their sulfation patterns. Nucleotide-sugar transporters and the nucleocytoplasmic O-GlcNAc cycle of OGT and OGA complete the picture, linking nutrient status to signalling.

Tyrosine catabolism disposes of the aromatic amino acid taken in from diet and protein turnover, converting it in the liver and kidney to fumarate and acetoacetate that feed the citric acid cycle and ketogenesis. The route runs through transamination to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate by tyrosine aminotransferase, dioxygenase-mediated conversion to homogentisate by HPD, ring cleavage by homogentisate dioxygenase, isomerization by the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and final hydrolysis by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Blocks at each step cause recognizable inherited disease: HPD or FAH deficiency gives tyrosinemia with hepatorenal damage from accumulated reactive intermediates, while loss of homogentisate dioxygenase causes alkaptonuria, in which homogentisate polymerizes and pigments cartilage. IL4I1, an L-amino acid oxidase secreted by myeloid cells, oxidizes tyrosine and other aromatic amino acids in the immune microenvironment rather than for energy, linking this chemistry to local amino acid depletion and T cell suppression.

Whether a muscle cell contracts, how strongly and how fast, is set by processes that tune calcium delivery to the sarcomere and the sensitivity of the sarcomere to it; this regulation of muscle contraction covers cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle alike. It determines cardiac output and rhythm, vascular tone and blood pressure, gut and airway motility, and skeletal muscle force, and its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia-type disorders and hypertension. Voltage-gated calcium and sodium channels, potassium and pacemaker channels, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum release and uptake machinery (ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps with phospholamban, calsequestrin, triadin and junctophilins) shape the calcium transient, while troponins, tropomyosin, myosin light chains and their kinases translate it into force. Layered on top are G protein-coupled inputs from adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting through cyclic nucleotides, calmodulin and RhoA, plus transcriptional and microRNA control of the contractile programme.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae, and organizing that folded surface is what gives oxidative phosphorylation the membrane area and local environment it needs. This pathway builds, shapes and remodels those folds and the contact sites that anchor them to the outer membrane. A core of MICOS subunits including IMMT, CHCHD3 and CHCHD6 defines crista junctions and, with SAMM50 and metaxins, bridges to the outer membrane as a tethering complex. Dynamin-family OPA1 controls inner membrane fusion and crista shape and is cleaved by the proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2 in response to stress or loss of membrane potential. Small TIM chaperones and the TIM22 and OXA1L insertases deliver and insert carrier and respiratory-chain proteins into the bilayer, while TAFAZZIN remodels cardiolipin, the lipid that stabilizes curvature and the complexes embedded in it.

Sensory perception covers the machinery by which the nervous system captures a physical or chemical stimulus, transduces it into an electrical signal, and encodes its quality and intensity. The gene list spans the major modalities: visual phototransduction through rhodopsin and cone opsins, transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase subunits, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the retinoid cycle enzymes that regenerate chromophore; a very large olfactory receptor repertoire with its trafficking cofactors and the vomeronasal and trace-amine receptors; sweet, umami and bitter taste receptors coupled to gustducin and PLC signalling; hair-cell mechanotransduction and stereocilia architecture via myosins, cadherin 23, protocadherin 15, usherin and whirlin; and somatosensory channels such as TRPV1, TRPM8, PIEZO2 and sensory sodium channels for pain, temperature and touch. Also present are lens crystallins and eye and ear developmental transcription factors. Failure of these components produces retinal degeneration, inherited deafness, cataract, anosmia and congenital insensitivity to pain.

Skeletal muscle repairs itself by recruiting mononucleate myoblasts to the site of injury, where they fuse either into surviving damaged fibres or with one another to build new myotubes. This fusion step is what converts a pool of committed precursors into multinucleated, contractile fibres, and it is the point at which regeneration produces functional tissue rather than merely more cells. The membrane chemistry is carried out by dedicated muscle fusogens: myomaker, a multipass transmembrane protein, acts with the small myomerger protein to bring apposed myoblast membranes together and drive them through hemifusion to full pore formation. Tetraspanins CD9 and CD81, together with their partner PTGFRN, organise the membrane microdomains in which cell–cell contact and fusion are coordinated. The process links satellite cell activation and myogenic differentiation to the restoration of fibre mass after damage.

Microautophagy is the route by which cytosolic material is taken directly into a late endosome or lysosome, without first being wrapped in an autophagosome: the limiting membrane of the degradative compartment invaginates around the cargo, pinches off inward, and the resulting single-membrane vesicle is broken down inside. It gives cells a continuous, low-cost way to turn over soluble proteins and portions of organelles, contributing to amino acid supply during nutrient stress and to quality control of the endolysosomal system itself. Much of the machinery is shared with other forms of autophagy: the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with RB1CC1 and ATG13, the ATG7- and ATG5-ATG12-ATG16L1-dependent lipid conjugation system, ATG4 proteases that process and recycle the conjugated protein, and the lipid-mobilising ATG2 and ATG9 proteins. ESCRT-associated VPS4A and VPS4B ATPases provide the membrane scission step that releases the internalised vesicle.

Attaching a phosphate group to threonine residues in proteins is one of the main reversible switches cells use to change enzyme activity, binding partners and protein stability. This collection captures peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation, the transfer of phosphate from ATP onto threonine hydroxyls by serine/threonine kinases, and the regulators and substrates that surround them. Represented here are cell cycle kinases such as CDK1 and the DNA damage checkpoint kinase CHEK1, growth and survival signalling through AKT1 and MAPK1, stress-activated JNK, the energy-sensing kinase STK11 and its downstream network, innate immune signalling via TBK1, and the WNK-SPAK arm that governs cation-chloride cotransporters and ion balance. Transcription factors including ATF2 appear as targets, showing how threonine phosphorylation converts signals into altered gene expression. The theme links proliferation control, metabolic sensing, cytoskeletal and junctional organisation, and responses to damage and infection.

DNA strand elongation is the extension step of genome duplication, in which nucleotides are added to the 3' end of a growing strand behind an advancing replication fork. Replicative polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon carry out priming and processive synthesis, the sliding clamp PCNA with its RFC loader keeps them engaged, DNA2 helps process Okazaki fragment flaps, and LIG1 seals the resulting nicks, while MCM subunits provide the helicase activity that exposes template strands. Elongation also occurs in specialised contexts represented here: telomerase reverse transcriptase extends chromosome ends, with POT1 and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex acting on telomeric and broken DNA. The INO80 complex, built around the INO80 ATPase together with RUVBL1/RUVBL2 and several ARP and accessory subunits, links nucleosome remodelling to replication, connecting chromatin state with the progression of synthesis through S phase.

Bone morphogenetic protein signalling has to be held in check for tissues to pattern correctly, and this negative regulation of the BMP pathway collects the brakes that do it. They act at every level: secreted antagonists such as noggin, chordin, gremlins, sclerostin and the Cerberus/DAN family sequester ligands before they reach receptors; BAMBI provides a decoy receptor; inhibitory Smads SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the E3 ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2 to degrade receptors and signalling Smads; phosphatases and transcriptional corepressors of the SKI/SKIL and SKOR families blunt the nuclear response; and a set of microRNAs tunes component levels. Restraint of this kind sets skeletal patterning and bone mass, limits ectopic cartilage and bone formation, and shapes dorsoventral axis formation in the early embryo. The same circuitry feeds into hepatic hepcidin control, where TMPRSS6 dampens BMP-driven signalling and its loss causes iron-refractory iron deficiency anaemia.

Epithelia line every body surface and duct, and this pathway covers how an unspecialized progenitor takes on epithelial identity: apical-basal polarity, junctional sealing, and the terminal specializations of skin, gut, kidney, airway, lens, hair and inner ear. Its outputs are the barrier that keeps water in and microbes out, the absorptive and secretory surfaces of the viscera, and the ciliated and sensory epithelia; failure produces ichthyosis and other cornification disorders, ciliopathies, deafness, cataract and loss of the differentiation controls whose collapse underlies carcinoma and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Lineage transcription factors such as GRHL2, KLF4, FOXA1, CDX2 and OVOL family members act downstream of Wnt, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog and Hippo cues, driving keratin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope genes, transglutaminase crosslinking, claudin and tight-junction assembly, and cell-cycle exit through CDKN1A and CDKN1B.

Myosin filament organization covers the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of the thick filaments built from myosin molecules, the structures that generate contractile force in muscle and other motile cells. Getting myosin into ordered filaments, and anchoring them within the contractile apparatus, is what allows a cell to translate ATP hydrolysis into directed shortening. The genes here span both striated and smooth muscle solutions to that problem: titin acts as a molecular ruler and scaffold along the thick filament, with telethonin binding its N-terminal region at the Z-disc, while smooth muscle myosin heavy chain supplies the filament-forming motor itself. Regulatory input comes from a kinase acting on myosin regulatory light chain and myosin phosphatase, coupling filament behaviour and contractility to signalling, and a Rho-family GDP dissociation stimulator links small GTPase activity to this cytoskeletal arrangement.

TOR signaling is the cell's master decision point on whether conditions favour growth: the mTOR kinase integrates amino acid supply, glucose and energy status, oxygen and growth factor input, and converts a favourable verdict into protein synthesis, lipid and nucleotide production, and suppression of autophagy. Two complexes carry the output, one built on RPTOR that phosphorylates S6 kinases and the 4E-BP translation repressors, the other on RICTOR. Amino acids are sensed at the lysosome, where the Ragulator scaffold and Rag GTPases position the kinase, with GATOR components, FLCN and sensors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR tuning the response; the TSC1/TSC2 complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein toward RHEB, and AMPK and LKB1 impose energy restraint. Loss of these brakes causes tuberous sclerosis and related hamartoma syndromes, and pathway hyperactivation is common in cancer, epilepsy and metabolic disease.

Cells that meet a microbe, an injury or a chemotactic gradient must not only detect it but amplify the reaction, and this collection of positive regulators of the response to external stimuli is what raises the gain. It underpins innate immune defence, inflammation, wound healing and leukocyte recruitment, and its over-activity produces septic shock, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like and RIG-I-like families feed through adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1, MAVS and STING1 into IRAK and TBK1 kinases, NF-kB and interferon-regulatory factors, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 mature IL-1B and IL-18 and drive gasdermin-mediated lytic death. Complement factors, ficolins, chemokines and their receptors, growth factors, coagulation proteins and many ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and microRNAs tune the strength and duration of the response.

Release of the gonadotropins LH and FSH from pituitary gonadotropes is the step that links the brain to the gonads, driving follicle maturation, ovulation, steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis; when it fails the result is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed or absent puberty and infertility. Hypothalamic kisspeptin, acting with neurokinin B and its receptor and with opioid signalling, paces the pulsatile GnRH drive that gonadotropes read through GnRH receptor, while RFRP peptide encoded by NPVF restrains it and leptin reports whether energy stores can support reproduction. Both hormones share the common alpha subunit CGA. Gonadal feedback is supplied by activin and inhibin subunits signalling through SMAD4, which oppose each other to set FSH output. FOXL2 contributes to this transcriptional control, and gap-junctional coupling through connexin 43 coordinates the secreting cells.

Signalling is limited as much by removing receptors as by activating them, and receptor catabolism is the route by which surface and internalised receptors are delivered to lysosomes and destroyed rather than recycled. It sets how long a cell can respond to a hormone, growth factor or neurotransmitter, and it underlies specific physiology: hepcidin binding triggers degradation of the iron exporter ferroportin, PCSK9 routes the LDL receptor to lysosomal destruction, and the MYLIP ubiquitin ligase acts on the same receptor. Mechanistically, HECT and RING ligases such as NEDD4, ITCH, SMURF1, RNF43 and ZNRF3 mark receptors with ubiquitin; ESCRT and sorting components including MVB12A, SNX25 and KIF16B carry cargo into multivesicular bodies; and BECN1, UVRAG, PIK3R4 and SH3GLB1 supply the phosphoinositide and autophagy-related machinery that completes lysosomal delivery, with proteases such as legumain and calpain finishing the job.

Integrins switch between low- and high-affinity states, and this pathway covers the signals that push them toward the adhesive state and so increase binding to extracellular matrix and to counter-receptors on other cells. It matters wherever cells must grip before they act: platelets aggregating at a wound through beta3 integrin, leukocytes arresting on endothelium under flow in response to chemokines such as CCL5, CCL21 and CXCL13, and lymphocytes stabilising contacts during antigen recognition. Inside-out activation runs from receptors and immune adaptors -- SYK, SKAP1, the T cell receptor chain CD3E, the platelet ADP receptor P2RY12 -- to the integrin cytoplasmic tail, where kindlin-1 binding promotes activation; FAK and Rac signalling then couple engaged integrins to cytoskeletal reinforcement and spreading. Mechanical input through PIEZO1 and growth factor cues feed in. Loss of such regulation produces bleeding disorders, fragile skin and defective immune cell trafficking.

High-density lipoprotein particles are not static: their protein and lipid cargo is continuously rebuilt, and this remodeling sets how much cholesterol they can carry back from tissues to the liver. It underlies reverse cholesterol transport, and variation in its components shifts HDL cholesterol levels and atherosclerosis risk. Apolipoprotein A-I and A-II provide the structural scaffold, with A-IV, C-I, C-III, E and M exchanging on and off; ABCG1 effluxes cellular cholesterol to mature particles; LCAT esterifies cholesterol to drive maturation from discoidal to spherical forms. Cholesteryl ester transfer protein swaps cholesteryl esters for triglyceride with apoB-containing lipoproteins, phospholipid transfer protein redistributes surface lipid, and hepatic, endothelial and lipoprotein lipases plus phospholipases hydrolyse the core and shell, shrinking particles and releasing fatty acids. Scavenger receptor B1 completes the route by delivering cholesteryl esters into hepatocytes and steroidogenic cells.

Erythropoietin is the kidney-derived hormone that sets the rate of red cell production, and the cellular response to it keeps erythroid progenitors alive, dividing, and differentiating into haemoglobin-filled erythrocytes. Loss of this signalling causes the anaemia of chronic kidney disease, while excessive or constitutive activation underlies polycythaemia; recombinant erythropoietin is used clinically precisely because this axis is rate-limiting. The hormone binds its dimeric receptor on progenitor surfaces, activating the associated tyrosine kinase JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT5 for transport to the nucleus and transcription of survival and proliferation genes; CREB1 contributes further transcriptional output. Stem cell factor signalling through the receptor KIT acts alongside this pathway during progenitor expansion, and RHEX is an erythropoietin-induced regulator of human erythroblast growth. The response therefore couples systemic oxygen sensing to marrow output, linking hormone-driven gene expression to blood cell homeostasis.

Midbrain dopaminergic neurons must send axons along stereotyped routes to the striatum and cortex, and this guidance step steers their growth cones toward those targets by reading attractive and repulsive cues in the surrounding tissue. The genes here mark Wnt-based guidance: secreted ligands such as WNT5A and WNT7B act through the Frizzled receptor FZD3 and the atypical tyrosine kinase-like receptor RYK, while the adhesion GPCR CELSR3 and the planar cell polarity protein VANGL2 provide the polarity machinery that converts a graded cue into directional turning and correct anterior-posterior orientation of the growing axon. The same components organise other longitudinal axon tracts, so this is a specialised use of planar polarity signalling rather than a dedicated dopaminergic system. Its output is the wiring layout of the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic projections on which dopaminergic neurotransmission depends.

Cells with identical genomes maintain different expression programmes because chromatin itself carries heritable information, and this is the machinery that writes, reads, erases and propagates it. Such epigenetic regulation of gene expression establishes lineage identity, silences repetitive and parasitic DNA, imprints maternal and paternal alleles, inactivates one X chromosome, and keeps the settings stable through rounds of DNA replication even after the initiating signal is gone. The components span DNA methylation writers and the TET dioxygenases that initiate demethylation, methyl-CpG readers such as MECP2 and UHRF1, histone acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC and sirtuin deacetylases, H3K9 and H3K27 methyltransferases with Polycomb and HP1 silencing complexes, ATP-dependent nucleosome remodellers, histone variants and linker histones, and a piRNA-guided arm that silences transposons in germ cells. Misdirection of these activities underlies imprinting disorders, Rett syndrome, and widespread silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer.

Anagen is the active growth phase of the hair cycle, the years-long period in which the follicle regenerates a bulb, proliferates matrix keratinocytes and extrudes a new shaft; scalp hair spends most of its life here, and the length of anagen sets how long hair can grow. Entry into and maintenance of this phase depends on Wnt signalling between dermal papilla and epithelium: WNT10B and WNT5A are expressed in the regenerating follicle, and canonical signalling through β-catenin (CTNNB1) is required for follicle fate and cycling, with stabilizing mutations causing pilomatrix tumours. The set also touches follicle structural integrity, since FERMT1 links basal keratinocytes to their matrix and SPINK5 restrains epidermal proteases; loss of either produces fragile skin with hair and desquamation defects. Failure to sustain anagen underlies alopecia, while chemotherapy damages precisely these rapidly dividing anagen follicles.

When DNA damage is detected, p53 launches a transcriptional cascade that arrests the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis; this pathway covers the brakes applied to that cascade, restraining or terminating p53 signalling so that responses are proportionate and reversible once damage is resolved. The central node is MDM2, the ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation and keeps its basal level low. Other routes act on p53 covalently or transcriptionally: SIRT1 deacetylates p53 to blunt its activity, KDM1A demethylates p53 at a lysine that governs its interaction with coactivating partners, DYRK-family kinases and proteasome-associated regulators modulate its turnover, and the mesenchymal transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 oppose the arrest and death programmes p53 drives. Excessive damping of this checkpoint allows damaged cells to proliferate, a route to tumour progression and therapy resistance exploited in many cancers.

Blood and lymphatic vessels are lined by a single sheet of flattened cells, and endothelial cell differentiation is how mesodermal, bone marrow or neural crest precursors acquire that identity. It determines whether vessels form at all, whether they become arterial, venous or lymphatic, and whether the barrier they present to blood is tight or leaky. Lineage specification runs through transcription factors such as ETV2, SOX17/SOX18, NR2F2 and PROX1, downstream of VEGFA signalling via KDR and NRP1, Notch-Delta/Jagged input with HEY1/HEY2, and BMP/TGF-beta receptors including ACVRL1, BMPR2 and SMAD4. Maturation brings the junctional and adhesion apparatus that defines the endothelium -- VE-cadherin, PECAM1, claudin-5 and the tight junction scaffolds -- plus Rap1 and Rho-kinase control of barrier tone and numerous microRNAs tuning the programme. Failure or corruption of these steps underlies cerebral cavernous malformation, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and pathological angiogenesis in tumours.

GTP metabolism covers the reactions that make, interconvert and consume guanosine triphosphate, the nucleotide that fuels ribosome function, tubulin assembly, membrane traffic and the switching of regulatory GTPases. Synthesis begins with IMP dehydrogenase, which commits inosine monophosphate to the guanine branch of purine biosynthesis and is the target of immunosuppressive drugs, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinase family transfers phosphate to GDP to keep GTP pools charged in cytosol and mitochondria. Mitochondrial GTP:AMP phosphotransferases use GTP as a phosphate donor for AMP, linking guanine and adenine nucleotide pools. Consumption is represented by the hydrolysing switches themselves: Ran for nucleocytoplasmic transport, Rab and Rho family members for vesicle and cytoskeletal control, translation factor GTPases, and the mitochondrial dynamics GTPases mitofusin and OPA1 that drive fusion of outer and inner membranes.

Rhythmic processes generate and maintain the periodic behaviour of physiology, from the roughly 24-hour circadian cycle to reproductive and seasonal rhythms. At the core sits a transcription-translation feedback loop in which CLOCK and BMAL1 drive expression of PER and CRY genes, whose products feed back to repress their own activators; casein kinases CSNK1D/CSNK1E and the ubiquitin ligase adaptor FBXL3 set the pace by controlling repressor phosphorylation and degradation. Nuclear receptors including RORA, NR1D1 and NR1D2 form a second interlocking loop, and chromatin modifiers, SIRT1 and NAMPT couple the clock to metabolic state. Output arms reach light input through opsins and retinal genes, melatonin synthesis via AANAT and MTNR1 receptors, and hypothalamic-pituitary hormone axes through GNRH1, GHRH and leptin signalling, so that timing information is distributed to sleep-wake, feeding, endocrine and cell-cycle machinery.

Positive chemotaxis is the steering of a motile cell up a chemical gradient, and it underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, immune surveillance and axon guidance. Without accurate attraction, leukocytes fail to reach infected or injured tissue, new vessels do not sprout toward hypoxic regions, and growing axons miss their targets; the same cues are co-opted by tumour cells to invade and by leukocytes to sustain chronic inflammation. The attractants here span several families: chemokines such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL12, CXCL8 and CX3CL1 acting on G protein-coupled receptors; VEGF family ligands with KDR and the co-receptor NRP1 drawing endothelial tip cells; HGF through MET and neurotrophic factors such as GDNF, ARTN and NTF3 guiding epithelial and neuronal migration; plus defensins, alarmins including HMGB1 and MIF, and formyl peptide sensing via FPR2. Downstream, cytoskeletal and polarity regulators including CORO1A and SCRIB convert the gradient into directed protrusion.

Touch, hearing, balance and mechanical pain all begin with the conversion of a physical force into an electrical signal, and this is the machinery that performs that transduction as the first step of sensory perception. Its failure produces congenital deafness, vestibular dysfunction, loss of proprioception and altered pain thresholds. Hair cells of the inner ear supply one arm: TMC1 and TMC2 with LHFPL5 and the tip-link and stereocilia proteins whirlin, PDZD7, stereocilin, PTPRQ and ADGRV1 gate current when the hair bundle deflects, while PJVK protects against noise damage. In somatosensory neurons, PIEZO2 mediates light touch and proprioception, TRPA1 responds to irritants and mechanical insult, and acid-sensing channels ASIC2 and ASIC3 contribute to mechanosensitivity. Voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A set excitability downstream, and growth factor and inflammatory signals such as NTRK1 and TNF tune sensitivity during injury.

Mitotic sister chromatid separation is the irreversible step at anaphase onset when paired chromatids, held together since replication, are physically detached and pulled to opposite poles, so that each daughter cell inherits one complete genome. Failure produces aneuploidy, micronuclei and chromosome instability of the kind that drives tumour progression. Cohesin, including its RAD21 subunit, is cleaved by the separase protease ESPL1; separase is held inactive until the anaphase-promoting complex, activated by CDC20, triggers destruction of its inhibitor and of cyclin B. Timing is enforced by the spindle assembly checkpoint at unattached kinetochores, where MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1, BUB3 and the NDC80 and RZZ complexes restrain CDC20 until every chromosome is bioriented; TRIP13 and USP44 tune checkpoint silencing. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin corrects faulty attachments, while dynein motors and PLK1 contribute to poleward movement.

Neurotransmitter release and uptake are held in check as well as driven, and this pathway collects the brakes: processes that reduce or block the movement of transmitters into, out of, and between cells, whether through vesicle fusion or through membrane transporters. Damping release matters for setting synaptic strength, preventing excitotoxic glutamate accumulation, and shaping short-term plasticity, and several of the genes involved are tied to neurological disease. Synaptotagmin-11 acts as an inhibitory clamp on vesicle exocytosis, in contrast to the calcium sensor synaptotagmin-1 that triggers it, while alpha-synuclein and parkin are central to Parkinson disease and to presynaptic protein homeostasis. Nitric oxide synthase provides diffusible retrograde signalling back onto terminals, PNKD is mutated in paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia, and zinc handling by SLC30A1 links metal availability to transmitter traffic.

Sodium is the dominant extracellular cation, and keeping its concentration within narrow limits sets cell volume, membrane excitability, extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. Maintaining that steady state depends on transporters and on the hormones that tune them. The Na+/K+-ATPase catalytic and beta subunits, together with their FXYD regulators, establish the transmembrane gradient that all secondary sodium-coupled transport exploits; NHE-family exchangers couple sodium entry to proton extrusion and thus to intracellular pH, while NKCC and NCC cotransporters and the epithelial sodium channel subunits reabsorb filtered sodium along the nephron. Superimposed on this are the renin-angiotensin and aldosterone-synthesizing arms, natriuretic peptide signalling through its guanylate cyclase receptor, and endothelin, which respectively promote or oppose sodium retention. Disruption produces salt-sensitive hypertension, renal salt-wasting or pseudohypoaldosteronism, and, through the neuronal ATPase subunits, familial migraine and dystonia-parkinsonism.

TGF-beta, BMP, activin and nodal ligands all converge on SMAD transcription factors, and the strength, duration and outcome of that relay is tuned at every step. This regulation shapes skeletal and cartilage patterning, vascular and cardiac development, iron homeostasis through hepcidin induction, and fibrotic and immune responses; its failure underlies hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, pulmonary arterial hypertension, skeletal dysplasias and tumour progression. Control operates through secreted antagonists such as noggin, gremlin and twisted gastrulation that sequester BMPs, co-receptors including endoglin and betaglycan that set ligand access to type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors, and inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 with the repressor SKI acting inside the cell. PMEPA1 and PIN1 modify receptor-activated SMAD stability and trafficking, while numerous microRNAs damp pathway components post-transcriptionally, giving graded rather than switch-like responses to ligand.

The mammary ductal tree is built by branching morphogenesis, in which epithelial ducts elongate from the nipple through the fat pad and bifurcate to fill it, creating the architecture that later supports alveolar differentiation and milk delivery. Without it the gland remains rudimentary and cannot lactate; the same growth and branching controls, when deregulated, underlie much of breast cancer biology. Steroid hormone receptors for estrogen, progesterone, androgen and vitamin D read systemic endocrine cues and act largely through paracrine relays, with amphiregulin acting as the estrogen-induced signal from luminal cells to surrounding stroma. Macrophage and eosinophil recruitment via CSF1 and CCL11 supplies stromal support at the invading end buds, while WNT4 and WNT5A, TGFB1, receptor tyrosine kinases such as EPHA2 and DDR1, SRC kinase, and transcriptional regulators including TBX3, ETV5 and TFAP2C set where a duct branches and where branching is suppressed.

Androgen receptor signalling turns testosterone and dihydrotestosterone into changes in gene transcription, and this regulatory layer sets how strongly and how long that output runs. The receptor is a ligand-activated transcription factor, so most control is exerted at chromatin and on receptor stability: acetyltransferase and deacetylase activities such as EP300, HDAC1 and SIRT1, demethylases including KDM1A and KDM4C, the arginine methyltransferase PRMT2, and the chromatin remodelling ATPase SMARCA4 tune the receptor's transcriptional competence, while the corepressors NCOR1 and NCOR2 and the zinc finger repressor ZBTB7A damp it. Ubiquitin ligases such as RNF6 and RNF14 and the deubiquitinase USP26 act on receptor turnover and coactivator recruitment, and SUMO conjugation via PIAS2 adds a further brake. Kinase and growth-factor inputs, including PKN1 and IGF1, couple the pathway to signals arriving from outside the cell, making androgen responses in prostate, muscle and other target tissues context dependent.

Although framed as control over the extent of cell growth, the genes here describe how neurons set and limit the size of their outgrowths — axon and dendrite extension, growth cone advance, and the decision to stop. This determines wiring during development and constrains regrowth after injury, where inhibitory cues make the difference between a repaired and a permanently severed tract. Guidance ligands and their receptors — semaphorins with plexins and neuropilin, netrin with DCC, slits, ephrins with EPH receptors — converge on Rho-family GTPase signalling through PAK1 and LIMK1 to remodel actin, while MAP1B, MAPT, CLASP2 and tubulin-modifying activity govern microtubule invasion of the growth cone. Trophic input from NGF, BDNF and their receptors, plus WNT and GSK3B, biases growth toward extension, whereas myelin-associated MAG and RTN4 acting through RTN4R impose the collapse and stalling that caps outgrowth.

Where a cell puts its centrosome determines where microtubules radiate from, and therefore which way the cell divides, migrates or extends a cilium. Positioning of the microtubule organizing center is the active process that moves this hub to a defined site and holds it there — apposed to the nucleus, beneath the cortex at a polarity cue, or docked at the plasma membrane. Dynein and its regulators NDE1, NDEL1 and PAFAH1B1 pull on microtubules to draw the centrosome toward cortical or nuclear anchor points, while LINC complex components SUN1, SUN2 and the nesprins SYNE1 and SYNE2 bridge the nuclear envelope to the cytoskeleton. Cortical partners such as GPSM1-family signalling, DLG1 and ezrin set the target site, AURKA and DLGAP5 couple positioning to mitotic progression, and CEP83 with IFT20 links the centriole to ciliary docking and transport.\n

N-acylethanolamines are fatty acid amides of ethanolamine that act as local lipid mediators: anandamide engages cannabinoid receptors, while palmitoylethanolamide and oleoylethanolamide signal largely through nuclear receptors to dampen inflammation and pain and to suppress feeding. Their metabolism sets how much of each mediator is available at a given tissue site. Production begins with membrane N-acyl-phosphatidylethanolamines, which a phospholipase D-type enzyme cleaves directly to release the free N-acylethanolamine; glycerophosphodiesterase activities provide an alternative multi-step route through glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine intermediates. Signal termination is hydrolytic, with an acid ceramidase-related amidase degrading these amides to fatty acid and ethanolamine, favouring the saturated and monounsaturated species in lysosomes of macrophages and other cells. The balance of synthesis and breakdown therefore shapes endocannabinoid tone, inflammatory resolution, and energy-balance signalling.

Vitamin D acts largely by changing gene expression, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly that happens. Tuning it determines calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, epithelial differentiation and immune tone; loss of receptor function causes hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, while excess signalling drives hypercalcaemia. Control begins upstream of the receptor itself: CYP27B1, the renal 1α-hydroxylase, generates the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and so dictates how much ligand is available. The liganded vitamin D receptor then heterodimerises with retinoid X receptors on target response elements, where coregulators such as MED1, SNW1, TRIM24 and MN1 modulate transactivation, and factors including KANK2 and the transcriptional repressor SNAI2 alter the magnitude or direction of the response.
