Cadmium has no biological use but enters cells through transporters built for iron, zinc and manganese, where it damages proteins and triggers oxidative stress. Detoxification of cadmium ion is the set of processes that limit that damage by binding the metal or moving it away from vulnerable compartments. A metallothionein provides high-affinity thiol coordination that sequesters the ion in an inert complex, while membrane transporters partition it: an efflux carrier of the zinc exporter family removes cytosolic metal, a divalent metal transporter of the macrophage-associated family handles uptake and vesicular handling, and an ABC transporter directs porphyrin and metal conjugate traffic into an intracellular compartment. The same carriers that import essential divalent metals are the route cadmium exploits, so this biology sits at the intersection of trace metal homeostasis and heavy-metal stress defence, and is relevant to kidney and lung injury caused by cadmium accumulation.

The nephric duct is the tube that drains the primitive kidney, and its initial formation sets up the plumbing from which the ureter, collecting system and, in males, parts of the reproductive tract derive. Epithelialisation of the intermediate mesoderm into a patent duct that extends caudally to insert into the cloaca depends on a small transcriptional and signalling module: PAX2 and GATA3 specify and maintain the nephric duct epithelium and guide its caudal extension, HNF1B shapes tubular epithelial identity, and BMP4 and WNT9B provide the surrounding instructive signals, with WNT9B later inducing metanephric mesenchyme. Failure or misrouting at this stage produces congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, including renal agenesis, duplex or ectopic ureters and vesicoureteral reflux, and mutations in these regulators cause inherited renal-coloboma and renal cyst syndromes.

Some viral messenger RNAs carry two open reading frames on one transcript, and termination-reinitiation is the trick that lets the downstream one be translated. Rather than dissociating completely when the ribosome stops at the upstream stop codon, a fraction of 40S subunits stay attached to the mRNA, scan or shift a short distance, and begin again at the start codon of the second cistron. This depends on host initiation machinery rather than anything virally encoded: multiple subunits of the eIF3 complex, including the scaffolding EIF3A and EIF3B and the cap-proximal EIF3D, are retained on the small subunit and help it recruit initiator tRNA again. Sequences upstream of the termination site in the viral RNA promote this retention. The result is expression of a protein that a strictly cap-dependent scanning mechanism would leave untranslated, expanding coding capacity from a compact genome.

Superoxide is both a weapon and a hazard, and this regulatory programme sets how much of it a cell makes and how fast it is disposed of. Tight control matters in two settings above all: the phagocyte respiratory burst that kills ingested microbes, and vascular and neuronal tissue, where excess superoxide oxidises lipids and proteins and drives inflammation, hypertension and neurodegeneration. Control is exerted at several levels — assembly and activation of the NADPH oxidase, with CYBA as a core membrane subunit and receptors such as CD36, CLEC7A, FPR2 and integrin CD11b/CD18 feeding through SYK, TYROBP and protein kinase C isoforms to trigger the burst; cofactor supply, where GCH1 governs tetrahydrobiopterin and thereby whether nitric oxide synthase produces NO or superoxide; and removal and antioxidant defence via SOD1 and NRF2-driven gene expression. Angiotensinogen, TGF-β1 and amyloid precursor protein link the pathway to hormonal and degenerative contexts.

The nervous system is built and, in some regions, renewed from a reservoir of neural stem cells that must divide without exhausting themselves, and neuronal stem cell population maintenance is the set of processes that keeps that reservoir intact. Too little self-renewal spends the progenitor pool early and yields a smaller brain; too much delays or blocks the production of neurons. Notch signalling through DLL1, JAG1 and NOTCH1 drives the HES1 and HES5 repressors that hold neighbouring cells undifferentiated, while SOX2 and the transcriptional repressor REST sustain stem cell identity and suppress premature neuronal gene expression. Cadherin-mediated adhesion holds progenitors in their niche, FOXO factors couple self-renewal to growth-factor and oxidative status, and centrosomal and microtubule-associated proteins including ASPM and MCPH1 govern progenitor divisions, with their loss causing primary microcephaly.

Amelogenesis is the ameloblast programme that builds tooth enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, and it proceeds in two phases: a secretory stage in which a protein-rich matrix is laid down and shaped, and a maturation stage in which that matrix is degraded and replaced by dense hydroxyapatite. Matrix proteins such as amelogenin, enamelin and amelotin set crystal orientation and thickness, while the proteases MMP20 and KLK4 remove the scaffold so mineral can fill the space. Mineralization depends on vectorial ion transport by ameloblasts, including calcium entry through store-operated channels, bicarbonate and chloride handling for pH buffering against acid released during crystal growth, and proton pumping, with FAM20A/FAM20C-dependent phosphorylation tuning matrix behaviour. Loss of these functions yields amelogenesis imperfecta, with thin hypoplastic or soft hypomineralized enamel prone to wear and caries.

Many cytokines, hormones and growth factors act on cells by routing their signal through STAT transcription factors, and this cell surface receptor signalling via STAT is the route by which immune polarisation, haematopoiesis, growth and metabolic status are translated into changed gene expression. Ligands and their receptors here span the interleukins, interferons, growth hormone, prolactin, erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and leptin; receptor engagement activates associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2), which phosphorylate STAT1 through STAT6, driving dimerisation, nuclear import and target promoter binding with coactivators such as EP300. Feedback and restraint are built in: SOCS and CISH proteins, PIAS1, and phosphatases including PTPN2 and PTPRC terminate the response, and several microRNAs tune it. Loss of individual components produces immunodeficiency, growth hormone insensitivity or defective antiviral defence, while constitutive STAT activity, particularly STAT3 and STAT5, supports leukaemias and solid tumour inflammation.

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by runaway peroxidation of membrane phospholipids rather than by caspases, and it shapes outcomes in neurodegeneration, ischemia-reperfusion injury and tumour cell survival. Mitochondria shrink with condensed densities and loss of cristae, and lethal reactive oxygen species accumulate from labile iron. The balance is set by cystine supply through the SLC7A11 antiporter feeding glutathione for GPX4, the peroxidase that reduces lipid hydroperoxides; AIFM2 provides a parallel, glutathione-independent defence at the membrane. ACSL4 biases membranes toward oxidizable polyunsaturated species, making cells more susceptible, while NFE2L2 drives an antioxidant and iron-handling programme including HMOX1, NQO1 and ferritin heavy chain. Iron storage, zinc and citrate transport, lipid and sterol synthesis, autophagic receptors such as SQSTM1, and energy sensing through AMPK all feed into whether a cell crosses the threshold.

Aerobic metabolism constantly leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and cellular oxidant detoxification is the set of reactions that removes them before they oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the redox tone in which signalling, proliferation and inflammation occur; its failure produces oxidative damage linked to neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, ageing and tumour promotion. Superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to peroxide in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space, and catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins then reduce peroxides, with thioredoxin, thioredoxin reductases, glutathione reductase and sulfiredoxin regenerating the oxidised catalysts. Glutathione transferases conjugate reactive electrophiles, several selenoproteins support thiol chemistry, and NFE2L2 drives transcription of many of these defences. Haem and metal-binding proteins sequester the iron and copper that would otherwise catalyse radical formation, while peroxidases such as MPO and TPO use peroxide productively in host defence and hormone synthesis.

Dendritic spines change shape when synapses change strength, and building, rearranging and dismantling the actin filament network on the postsynaptic side is what allows that to happen. Organization of the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton gives the spine head its structure, anchors receptor scaffolds beneath the membrane, and converts synaptic activity into lasting changes in spine size and number, the structural basis of synaptic plasticity. Actin isoforms provide the filaments themselves, while nucleation-promoting and regulatory proteins such as WASF2 and the small GTPase RAC3 drive branched polymerization, and MYH10 supplies non-muscle myosin contractility. Membrane-cytoskeleton linkers and adaptors including ezrin, DBNL, SH3GL2 and SRCIN1 couple filaments to the plasma membrane, endocytic machinery and signalling complexes, with NOS1AP tying nitric oxide synthase signalling to the same structures. The result is a locally remodelled compartment that is both a mechanical and a signalling platform.

Cytosolic RIG-I detects viral RNA and triggers interferon production; the genes here amplify that detection, raising the sensitivity and output of RIG-I signaling so that an antiviral state is established quickly after infection. This positive regulation matters because RIG-I sensing sets the threshold between rapid viral clearance and unchecked replication, and it must be tuned upward transiently without provoking interferon-driven autoinflammation. Several members act as cofactors that help load or stabilise RNA ligands on the sensor, including the helicases DDX60 and DHX58 and the zinc-finger protein ZCCHC3, while OASL mimics ubiquitin to enhance signalling and ZC3HAV1 engages viral RNA and downstream adaptors. Ubiquitin-pathway components such as USP15 and TRIM15 modulate the ubiquitination steps that license sensor oligomerisation and MAVS-dependent signalling, and RNA-binding regulators contribute post-transcriptional control. The output feeds into type I interferon induction and innate immune defence.

Before a dividing cell can copy its genome, each origin must be licensed once and only once, and this initiation step of cell cycle DNA replication is where that decision is made and executed. Getting it wrong produces under-replicated or re-replicated DNA, chromosome breakage and the genome instability that accompanies tumour formation. CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 hexameric helicase onto origin DNA during G1, and geminin binds and sequesters CDT1 after replication begins so that loaded origins cannot be relicensed within the same cycle. Once fired, the MCM ring unwinds duplex DNA ahead of the fork, and the polymerase alpha-primase catalytic subunit POLA1 lays down the RNA-DNA primers from which processive synthesis proceeds. The pathway therefore couples origin licensing to cell cycle position and is a target of checkpoint control and of replication-stress responses.

Opsonization is the tagging of microbes, immune complexes and dying cells with soluble molecules that mark them for recognition by phagocyte receptors, and the genes here set how much of that tagging occurs. Control over the process determines how efficiently pathogens and debris are cleared without damaging host tissue. The central event is deposition of C3 and C4 fragments on a surface. Pattern-recognition collectins and ficolins, together with MBL2, bind carbohydrate and acetylated ligands and activate the MASP proteases, while C2, factor B and properdin build and stabilise the convertases that amplify C3 cleavage. Opposing them, the C4b-binding protein subunits act as inhibitory regulators that accelerate decay of C4b-containing convertases and restrict labelling of self surfaces. The balance between these activating and restraining arms tunes complement output at the level of surface opsonin density.

Before an intron can be removed, the spliceosome must first identify its branch point, and U2-type prespliceosome assembly is that recognition step. It converts the early commitment complex on a pre-mRNA into the A complex, in which U2 snRNP is stably base-paired with the branch point sequence upstream of the 3' splice site, committing the intron to removal and fixing which splice sites will be joined. The machinery combines the Sm core proteins shared by all spliceosomal snRNPs with U2-specific subunits, the SF3A and SF3B multiprotein complexes that clamp the duplex and sequester the branch adenosine, and DEAD-box ATPases that supply the conformational proofreading needed for accurate site selection. Because this step sets splice-site choice, it is a control point for alternative splicing and a target of splicing-modulator compounds that bind SF3B1, whose mutation recurs in myelodysplastic syndromes.

Microvilli are the densely packed actin protrusions that expand the apical surface of absorptive epithelia, and this pathway covers the signals that promote their assembly rather than the structural core itself. The activating arm here runs through a small GTPase of the Ras superfamily, RAP2A, together with the guanine nucleotide exchange factors RAPGEF2 and RAPGEF6 that load it with GTP, and the STE20-family kinases STK26 (MST4) and TNIK that act as downstream or associated effectors. Kinase activity of this type links apical membrane cues to the actin machinery that elongates and bundles microvillar cores, placing the pathway at the junction of Rap GTPase signalling, epithelial apical organization and cytoskeletal remodelling. Positive regulation of microvillus assembly therefore determines how much specialized absorptive or sensory surface area a differentiating epithelial cell builds.

Purine nucleobase transmembrane transport moves adenine, guanine, hypoxanthine and related bases across membranes, supplying cells that cannot make purines de novo with the raw material for salvage into nucleotides. Because free bases and nucleosides are hydrophilic, they require carriers: the concentrative sodium-coupled nucleoside transporters of the SLC28 family drive uptake against a gradient using the sodium electrochemical gradient, while the equilibrative SLC29 carriers allow bidirectional, facilitated flux at the plasma membrane and, for SLC29A3, within intracellular membranes. SLC43A3 also contributes to nucleobase permeation, and AQP9, better known as a glycerol-permeable aquaglyceroporin, provides an additional low-selectivity route. Collectively this transport sets intracellular purine pools, supports nucleotide salvage and adenosine handling in tissues such as intestine, liver, kidney and blood cells, and governs cellular entry of nucleoside and nucleobase analogue drugs.

Lymphocytes only work if they reach the right tissue, and this pathway covers the signals that increase their movement out of blood and through lymphoid organs and inflamed sites. It underlies immune surveillance, germinal centre organisation and the recruitment of T and B cells to infection or tumour, and its dysregulation drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune infiltration. Chemokines and their receptors set the direction: CXCL12, CXCL13 and CCL21 guide homing to lymphoid niches, while CCL3, CCL5, CXCL10 and CCR2 dominate inflammatory recruitment. Adhesion and endothelial junction molecules including ITGA4, MADCAM1 and JAM2 mediate arrest and diapedesis, particularly gut homing. Inside the cell, RHOA, DOCK8, PTK2B, NEDD9 and the WNK1–OXSR1/STK39 kinase module control cytoskeletal polarity, volume regulation and motility, and ADAM proteases shed surface receptors to tune the response.

Mature microRNAs are not permanent: their abundance is set as much by how fast they are destroyed as by how fast they are made, and this pathway covers the factors that tune the rate of miRNA decay. Controlling turnover allows a cell to reset its repertoire of repressive small RNAs quickly during differentiation or in response to stimuli, rather than waiting out passive dilution. The regulators here act by several routes: ZSWIM8 is a substrate receptor of a ubiquitin ligase complex that triggers target-directed degradation of specific miRNAs, TENT2 adds nucleotides to miRNA 3' ends, and PNPT1 is an exoribonuclease-type activity acting on RNA. RNA-binding proteins such as LIN28B and QKI and long non-coding RNAs including NEAT1 and HOTTIP modulate the process by sequestering or presenting substrates, linking miRNA clearance to broader post-transcriptional gene regulation.

Cellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle imposed on damaged, stressed or oncogene-expressing cells, and the regulation of that decision determines whether a cell is arrested, killed, or allowed to keep dividing. Too little restraint contributes to tumour suppression failure; too much drives tissue ageing and the inflammatory secretory state of accumulated senescent cells. Control is exerted at several levels: telomere maintenance by telomerase and telomere-binding proteins sets replicative limits, the p53 axis and PTEN-PI3K signalling relay damage and growth cues, CDK6 and RBL1 act on the arrest machinery itself, and SIRT1, SIRT6 and the histone methyltransferase SUV39H1 impose chromatin changes that lock in the state. Cytosolic DNA sensing through CGAS links genome damage to inflammatory output, while numerous microRNAs tune the threshold. Prelamin A processing by ZMPSTE24 ties this to premature ageing syndromes.

Interferon gamma, released mainly by T cells and NK cells, converts responding cells into an antimicrobial and antigen-presenting state, and the genes it induces define that state. The response underlies clearance of intracellular bacteria, protozoa and viruses, drives tumour immune recognition, and when chronic contributes to autoimmunity, macrophage activation syndromes and immune checkpoint-mediated escape. Receptor engagement signals through JAK2 and STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF9 amplifying transcription, raising class I and class II MHC together with the peptide-loading machinery TAP1, TAPBP and the immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8 and PSMB9, and CIITA and NLRC5 as the transactivators that coordinate them. Downstream products include chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 that recruit lymphocytes, adhesion molecules, complement components, guanylate-binding proteins, IDO1-mediated tryptophan depletion, nucleic acid sensors, apoptotic effectors, and PD-L1 plus SOCS1 as brakes limiting the response.

Interferon signalling ends in the expression of hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes, and the antimicrobial mechanism of these genes is where the response actually blocks pathogen replication. Detection by cytosolic RNA sensors and their adaptor feeds through kinases and IRF3 to JAK1 and STAT1, and the induced effectors then attack distinct stages of the viral life cycle. Protein kinase R phosphorylates eIF2α to shut down cap-dependent translation initiation, which explains the many initiation factors and small ribosomal subunit proteins here; the oligoadenylate synthetases generate 2'-5'A to switch on RNase L and degrade cellular and viral RNA; IFIT proteins sequester non-self mRNA ends, MX GTPases trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins act against intracellular bacteria and parasites. ISG15 conjugation through UBA7, UBE2L6 and HERC5 modifies host and viral targets, with USP18 reversing it, while nucleoporins and importins control the trafficking on which these steps depend.

Several secreted proteins acquire calcium-binding ability only after a vitamin K-dependent modification made as they transit the secretory pathway. Gamma-carboxylation converts glutamate residues in an amino-terminal Gla motif into gamma-carboxyglutamate, which lets the mature protein bind calcium and dock onto membrane phospholipid surfaces; removal of the propeptide by a furin-type protease in the Golgi completes maturation. Most of the substrates run the coagulation cascade and its brakes — prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, together with the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z — so loss of the carboxylase or of its vitamin K cofactor produces bleeding disorders, and this chemistry is the target of warfarin-class anticoagulants. Other clients extend the theme beyond haemostasis: osteocalcin in bone mineralization and Gas6 in receptor tyrosine kinase signalling and apoptotic cell clearance.

Newly initiated RNA polymerase II transcripts are capped while still being made, and this step links the polymerase to the capping enzymes during transcription of the integrated HIV provirus. Capping protects the nascent 5' end from exonucleases and marks the transcript for export and translation, so viral mRNAs depend on it as host mRNAs do. The mechanism runs through the heptapeptide repeats of the largest polymerase subunit: the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7, with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners, phosphorylates serine 5 of the C-terminal domain near the promoter, and the phosphorylated tail is bound directly by the guanylyltransferase and the cap methyltransferase, which stimulates guanylyl transfer. The elongation factor SPT5 contributes to coupling capping with early elongation. This phosphorylation mark is the timing signal that restricts capping to polymerase II products.

TLR10 is an innate immune receptor of the Toll-like family expressed in a restricted way, mainly on B cells and dendritic cells, whose ligands remain poorly defined; it homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2, and signals through the MyD88 adaptor. The downstream cascade described here is the shared MyD88-dependent route that converts receptor engagement into inflammatory gene expression: IRAK4, IRAK1/2 and Pellino ligases assemble with TRAF6 and the TAK1-TAB complex, K63-linked ubiquitin chains built by UBE2N/UBE2V1 relay the signal, and the IKK complex frees NF-kB from IkB while parallel MAP kinase branches activate p38, JNK, ERK and the AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. DUSP phosphatases, PP2A subunits and deubiquitinases restrain the output. The result is cytokine production and antigen-presenting cell activation; TLR10 itself is generally regarded as a dampener of inflammatory TLR responses.

Influenza virus encodes no ribosomes of its own, so every viral protein is made by the host translation apparatus; this step converts spliced and unspliced viral mRNA in the cytoplasm into the roughly ten polypeptides that build new particles, including the surface glycoproteins HA and NA, the polymerase subunits PB1, PB2 and PA, nucleoprotein, matrix proteins and NS1. The bulk of the gene content is the cytoplasmic 40S and 60S ribosomal subunit proteins that carry out initiation and elongation. Conserved viral 5' untranslated sequences favour recruitment of this machinery, aided by the host G-rich sequence factor GRSF1, while the co-chaperone P58(IPK) restrains the antiviral kinase PKR so that initiation is not shut down by the interferon-induced translational block. Host protein synthesis falls at the same time, making this the point where the virus captures a central cellular process to its own ends.

Neurons are eliminated during development and after injury when the p75 neurotrophin receptor, rather than TrkA, dominates the response to nerve growth factor or its unprocessed precursor, and this receptor-initiated death programme is what the intracellular adaptors NRAGE, NRIF and NADE carry forward. It matters because it sculpts the size of neuronal populations to match their targets and contributes to neuronal loss after axotomy and in degenerative injury. Ligand-bound NGFR recruits TRAF6 and MAGED1 (NRAGE), engages Rac1 through an array of Rho-family exchange factors, and activates JNK, converging on BAD, BIM and caspase-3 to dismantle the cell. In parallel, gamma-secretase components including presenilins and nicastrin cleave the receptor so that its intracellular domain, with NRIF, can reach the nucleus and drive transcriptional events; ubiquitin and SQSTM1 support the signalling scaffold.

Nudix hydrolases keep the cellular nucleotide pool clean, and the phosphate bond hydrolysis they carry out is best understood as sanitation: damaged or surplus nucleotides are cleaved before they can be used as substrates. Oxidised, deaminated or methylated purine nucleoside di- and triphosphates are degraded by enzymes such as NUDT1, NUDT15 and NUDT18, preventing their incorporation into DNA as mutations or into mRNA as mistranslated protein. NUDT16 acts on inosine- and other modified guanine-containing nucleotides, while NUDT9 and NUDT5 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, limiting non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and the accumulation of a potent second messenger; ADPRM degrades ADP-ribose 1''-phosphate from tRNA splicing. Because these enzymes also destroy nucleotide analogues, their activity sets tolerance to thiopurine and other nucleoside-based chemotherapies, and NUDT15 variants cause severe drug toxicity.

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and cancers frequently escape that restraint by disabling the step at which the signal is written onto its transcription factors. Ligand-bound receptors, with SARA/ZFYVE9 presenting the substrate to the type I receptor kinase, phosphorylate the conserved Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif at the extreme C-terminus of SMAD2 and SMAD3; the final two serines (Ser465/Ser467 in SMAD2, Ser423/Ser425 in SMAD3) are the actual acceptor sites. Phosphorylation licenses heterotrimer formation with SMAD4 and nuclear transcription of growth-inhibitory targets. Tumour-derived mutants of this motif substitute the serines for residues that cannot accept phosphate, or delete and truncate the motif altogether, so the receptor complex remains competent but the effector cannot be activated and the cytostatic transcriptional response is lost. This is a loss-of-function mechanism within TGF-beta receptor signalling and tumour suppression.

Reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence both run on NADPH, and this route supplies it outside the mitochondrion by oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate. Cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1), which is also targeted to peroxisomes, carries out the NADP+-dependent step, giving both compartments a local source of reducing equivalents for fatty acid and sterol synthesis and for regenerating reduced glutathione and thioredoxin after oxidative stress; peroxisomes need it for reactions of beta-oxidation of unusual fatty acids. Aconitase (ACO1) feeds the reaction by interconverting citrate and isocitrate, linking the cytosolic pool of tricarboxylic acids to NADPH output; the same protein doubles as the iron-regulatory RNA-binding protein when its iron-sulfur cluster is lost. Cells short of this NADPH regeneration capacity become vulnerable to peroxide and to demands for lipid synthesis.

Extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP and adenosine act as signals reporting cell damage, stress and nucleotide release, and this family of nucleotide-like purinergic receptors is how cells read them. The set covers the G protein-coupled arm: four adenosine receptors that tune vascular tone, inflammation, neuronal excitability and cardiac rate, and the P2Y receptors that respond to nucleotides. Some couple through Gq to phospholipase C and calcium release, others through Gi to lower cyclic AMP, so a single nucleotide can produce opposing outcomes depending on which receptor a cell expresses. P2RY12 on platelets drives ADP-dependent aggregation and is the target of widely used antithrombotic drugs. Related orphan and lysophospholipid-responsive receptors are grouped here by sequence kinship. Collectively these receptors shape vascular reactivity, immune cytokine secretion, platelet activation and apoptotic responses to nucleotide release.

Smooth muscle contraction sets the tone of hollow organs and vessels, narrowing airways, gut, bladder and arteries without the striated banding of skeletal or cardiac muscle. It is driven by autonomic nerves, hormones, local chemical signals and mechanical load, and it is what allows these tissues to regulate their own diameter and wall tension. A rise in intracellular calcium is the trigger: calmodulin-bound myosin light chain kinase phosphorylates the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin, while caldesmon acts on the actin filament as a second, troponin-like control point. Force is transmitted through a distinctive cytoskeletal architecture, with smooth muscle actin and myosin heavy chain anchored via dense bodies and integrin-based focal adhesions containing talin, vinculin, paxillin and vinexin-family adaptors, so contraction squeezes the whole cell. Soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP phosphodiesterase activity provide the opposing relaxation arm.

Hedgehog signalling converts a secreted morphogen gradient into patterned gene expression, and it is what tells cells in the limb bud, neural tube and developing skeleton which position they occupy; in adults it maintains stem and progenitor compartments. Loss of output causes birth defects such as holoprosencephaly and polydactyly, while inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Ligands SHH, IHH and DHH are lipid-modified and released, then bind the receptor PTCH1, relieving its inhibition of Smoothened. Signalling is organised at the primary cilium, so intraflagellar transport components, the anterograde kinesin motor, retrograde dynein and tubulins are integral rather than incidental. In the off state, GPR161 raises cAMP and protein kinase A, GSK3 and casein kinase 1 prime GLI proteins for processing by the ubiquitin-proteasome system into repressors; SUFU sequesters them. Activation preserves full-length GLI activators, with SPOP, ITCH and SMURF ligases tuning the response.

Dishevelled proteins sit at the hub of WNT reception, and one way cells set the ceiling on WNT output is by sequestering them. This branch describes negative regulation of TCF-dependent signalling by DVL-interacting proteins: CXXC4 (Idax) and CCDC88C (DAPLE) bind DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 directly and dampen their ability to relay signal from activated receptors, so less beta-catenin escapes destruction and fewer TCF/LEF target genes are switched on. Because WNT/beta-catenin activity governs stem cell renewal, body axis patterning and tissue growth, restraint at the DVL step matters as much as activation does; loss of CCDC88C causes congenital hydrocephalus, and unchecked TCF-dependent transcription is a hallmark of colorectal tumourigenesis. DVL is also the point where canonical and planar-cell-polarity WNT branches diverge, so its interactors influence which route a WNT signal takes.

The plateau phase is the long depolarized shoulder of the cardiac action potential, and it is what gives heart muscle its extended refractory period and time to contract and eject blood. It arises from a near balance between inward and outward current: L-type calcium channels built around the CACNA1C pore-forming subunit with its auxiliary alpha2-delta, beta and gamma partners admit calcium that both sustains depolarization and triggers calcium-induced calcium release for contraction, while the slow delayed rectifier potassium channel formed by KCNQ1 with KCNE accessory subunits carries the opposing efflux that eventually allows repolarization. KCNE proteins tune gating kinetics and current amplitude, and the scaffold AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to KCNQ1 so that adrenergic stimulation can shorten the plateau as heart rate rises. The duration set here determines the QT interval and the timing of each beat.

Superoxide is made deliberately by NADPH oxidase complexes, and small GTPases of the RHO family are the switch that turns them on. When RAC1 or RAC2 loaded with GTP docks onto the membrane flavocytochrome and its cytosolic partners, electrons pass from NADPH to oxygen and superoxide is released into a phagosome or across the plasma membrane. In neutrophils this burst is the chemistry that kills ingested bacteria and fungi; loss of the catalytic subunit or of the p47/p67/p40 assembly causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent infection and granuloma formation. In endothelium the same output acts as a second messenger that amplifies VEGF receptor signalling during angiogenesis. Assembly is licensed by phosphorylation, with kinases including protein kinase C isoforms and ERK/p38 MAP kinases modifying the cytosolic factors, and S100A8/A9 and PIN1 contributing to subunit handling. Related oxidases NOX1 and NOX3 are activated through homologous adaptors.

Growth factor signalling through RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and negative regulation of the MAPK pathway is how the duration, amplitude and location of that signal are set. Without it, sustained ERK activity drives inappropriate proliferation and transformation, which is why many of these brakes are lost or bypassed in cancer. ERK itself feeds back onto RAF and onto MAP2K1 at T292, priming the PP2A holoenzyme and PP5 to strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region; subsequent phosphorylation restores 14-3-3 (YWHAB) binding and returns RAF to an autoinhibited state. PEBP1 sequesters RAF1 away from its MEK substrates, and scaffolds and modifiers such as KSR1, BRAP and PAQR3 constrain complex assembly and membrane localisation. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, many of them ERK-induced, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, closing the loop.

Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without any requirement for oxygen. It supplies the entire energy budget of cells lacking mitochondria, such as the mature erythrocyte, and is the metabolic mode that proliferating and hypoxic tissues, including tumours, lean on most heavily. Hexokinases and glucokinase commit glucose to the pathway; phosphofructokinase 1 catalyses the physiologically irreversible step that sets flux, itself tuned by the fructose-2,6-bisphosphate made and degraded by the bifunctional PFKFB enzymes; aldolase, triose phosphate isomerase, GAPDH, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the conversion to pyruvate. Under aerobic conditions NADH is reoxidised through the respiratory chain, while anaerobically pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+. Protein kinase A and protein phosphatase 2A subunits provide phosphorylation-based control. Deficiencies in pyruvate kinase or phosphoglycerate kinase cause haemolytic anaemia and myopathy.

Almost every eukaryotic mRNA acquires its mature 3' end after transcription, by endonucleolytic cleavage downstream of the coding sequence followed by addition of a long poly(A) tail; the downstream fragment is degraded and the two steps are tightly coupled. The tail determines mRNA stability, export competence and translational efficiency, so this processing is the step that converts a nascent transcript into a usable message. Recognition of the polyadenylation signal is carried out by the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor subunits together with WDR33, FIP1L1 and CPSF6/NUDT21, the cleavage stimulation factor subunits, symplekin and PCF11, with PAPOLA and PABPN1 building and measuring the tail and XRN2 clearing the released downstream RNA. The presence of RNA polymerase II subunits, spliceosomal and hnRNP/SR proteins, and export factors reflects how closely 3'-end formation is tied to transcription, splicing and termination in vivo. Major histone mRNAs are the exception, being cleaved but not polyadenylated.

Base excision repair handles the most common everyday damage to DNA ": oxidized, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionizing radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Without it, mutation rates rise and lesions such as 8-oxoguanine are mispaired during replication; loss of MUTYH predisposes to colorectal adenomatous polyposis, and the route is also how uracil and thymine glycol are cleared from the genome. Repair begins with one of several damage-specific glycosylases ": UNG, OGG1, NTHL1, SMUG1, TDG, MPG and the NEIL enzymes ": which cleave the glycosidic bond and leave an abasic site. APEX1 and PNKP process the resulting ends, then either POLB with XRCC1 and LIG3 fills a single nucleotide, or PCNA, RFC, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1 replace a longer patch. PARP1 and PARP2 signal the strand break and recruit the scaffold, and chromatin and telomere-binding proteins set the context in which this repair occurs.

Insulin binding to its receptor does not itself instruct the cell; the message is relayed through insulin receptor substrate proteins, and their activation is the step that converts receptor autophosphorylation into intracellular signalling. IRS1 docks on the activated receptor through its PTB domain, binding a phosphotyrosine in the juxtamembrane region, with its PH domain anchoring it to plasma membrane phospholipids so the receptor kinase can phosphorylate numerous tyrosines along the molecule. The phosphorylated IRS then dissociates from the receptor and serves as a membrane-proximal scaffold whose phosphotyrosines recruit SH2-domain partners, launching PI3K-dependent signalling toward glucose uptake and anabolic metabolism as well as the SOS-RAF-MAP kinase branch that drives growth and gene expression. IRS2 acts in parallel, and GRB10 is another receptor-associated adaptor at this node, making IRS activation the branch point of insulin action.

The mitochondrial genome is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, and mitochondrial rRNA processing is how the 12S and 16S rRNAs of the mitoribosome are cut out of that transcript and chemically finished. Because the mitochondrial genome encodes core subunits of the respiratory chain complexes and ATP synthase, the mitoribosome these rRNAs build is what allows those subunits to be made inside the organelle. Endonucleolytic release depends on a mitochondrial RNase P activity, assembled from a methyltransferase-like subunit, a dehydrogenase subunit and a catalytic protein partner, acting at tRNA 5' ends, with a separate enzyme trimming 3' ends; flanking tRNAs punctuate the transcript and so define the cleavage sites. Dedicated methyltransferases and pseudouridine synthases then modify a small number of nucleotides in each rRNA, while RNA-binding and transcription-termination-related factors organise the granules where processing and ribosome assembly occur.

Alanine metabolism in humans comes down to a single reversible reaction: the transfer of an amino group between alanine and 2-oxoglutarate to yield pyruvate and glutamate. This interconversion links protein turnover to energy metabolism, letting muscle export amino nitrogen as alanine to the liver, where the carbon skeleton re-enters gluconeogenesis and the nitrogen is routed toward urea synthesis. Two alanine aminotransferases carry it out, a cytosolic and a mitochondrial form, both pyridoxal phosphate-dependent, so the reaction can run on either side of the mitochondrial membrane according to the cell's redox and nitrogen load. The cytosolic enzyme is abundant in hepatocytes, and its release into plasma is the standard clinical indicator of liver injury. Loss of the mitochondrial enzyme causes a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder, underlining how this small piece of amino acid handling supports fuel supply beyond the liver.

Erythropoietin drives the survival and maturation of red blood cell precursors, and one branch of that signal works through phospholipase C gamma to convert receptor occupancy into a calcium and lipid second-messenger response. When erythropoietin binds its receptor, the associated kinase JAK2 is activated and the receptor becomes tyrosine phosphorylated; PLCG1 or PLCG2 docks there and is phosphorylated by the Src-family kinase LYN. The activated phospholipase then cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, which releases calcium from intracellular stores, and diacylglycerol, which recruits and activates protein kinase C. This arm complements the better-known STAT5 and PI3K outputs of the same receptor, feeding calcium- and PKC-dependent control of proliferation, differentiation and gene expression in erythroid progenitors responding to tissue oxygen demand.

Peroxisomes have no protein synthesis of their own, so every protein in their bounding membrane must be delivered from the cytosol; class I import is the route most of them take. Newly made peroxisomal membrane proteins are captured by the cytosolic receptor-chaperone PEX19, which recognises signals that include positively charged residues within the transmembrane segment, and are handed to PEX3 in the peroxisomal membrane, where insertion occurs without apparent nucleotide hydrolysis. PEX3 itself is a special case, docking instead with PEX16, and both can be inserted co-translationally into the endoplasmic reticulum, allowing ER- and mitochondria-derived vesicles to seed new peroxisomes alongside growth and division of existing ones. The cargoes delivered this way include the ABC transporters ABCD1-3, the docking and RING components of the matrix import machinery, and division factors such as PEX11B and FIS1.

NOTCH4 is expressed largely in endothelium, where the amount of its released intracellular domain reaching the nucleus sets the strength of Notch output during blood vessel development. Negative regulation of NOTCH4 signaling is how that output is limited, and it operates at two levels. AKT1-mediated phosphorylation of the intracellular fragment promotes its capture by 14-3-3 zeta (YWHAZ), holding it in the cytosol and away from target-gene promoters; the interacting protein TACC3 also dampens signaling. In parallel, the SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1, RBX1 and the substrate receptor FBXW7 ubiquitinates the phosphorylated fragment, after which the 26S proteasome, represented here by its full complement of core and regulatory subunits together with ubiquitin, destroys it. Loss of FBXW7 in mouse embryos raises this fragment and impairs vascular development, placing the pathway within ubiquitin-dependent proteolytic control of developmental signaling.

Drug absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion describes what the body does to a medicine: how it enters cells, where it travels, how it is chemically altered and how it leaves. This determines the dose and dosing interval that produce a useful concentration at a drug's target, and is distinct from the pharmacological action of the drug itself. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and cation families move compounds into hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, while efflux pumps such as ABCB1 and ABCG2 export them back out and limit tissue penetration. Cytochrome P450 enzymes including CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 carry out oxidative phase I metabolism; UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases and N-acetyltransferases conjugate the products for excretion. Esterases, purine salvage and nucleoside-metabolising enzymes activate or inactivate prodrugs such as thiopurines and nucleoside analogues, and plasma proteins such as albumin govern the free fraction available to act.

Blood clotting depends on a relay of plasma proteases and cofactors that converts fibrinogen to fibrin at a site of vessel injury, and this grouping collects the inherited defects of that cascade. Loss-of-function changes in factor VIII or factor IX cause haemophilia A and B, fibrinogen chain mutations give afibrinogenaemia and dysfibrinogenaemia, and von Willebrand factor defects impair platelet adhesion through the GPIb-IX-V receptor complex, whose subunits are themselves mutated in Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Failures of post-translational processing matter as much as the factors: vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX licenses calcium-dependent membrane binding, and tyrosine sulfotransferases modify factor VIII and related substrates. The balance runs both ways, since protein C and protein S defects, and gain-of-activity variants of factor V and factor IX, tip the system toward thrombophilia rather than bleeding. Scrambling of membrane phospholipid by ANO6 supports procoagulant surface exposure on platelets.

Complement amplifies itself: C3b generated by a convertase becomes part of another convertase, and the alternative pathway ticks over continuously through spontaneous C3 hydrolysis. Regulation of the complement cascade is what keeps this runaway chemistry pointed at pathogens and debris rather than at host tissue, and it also supports the routine clearance of dead cells and oxidative damage. A family of regulators of complement activation, built from tandem complement control protein repeats, works in two ways: decay-accelerating dissociation of the C3 and C5 convertases, exemplified by CD55, and cofactor activity for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b, provided by CR1, membrane cofactor protein CD46, factor H and, for C4b, C4b-binding protein. Additional brakes act elsewhere in the cascade, including C1 inhibitor on the classical initiation step, carboxypeptidase inactivation of the C3a and C5a anaphylatoxins, and CD59 restraint of the membrane attack complex.

Blood flowing over the apical surface of the vessel wall is a mechanical signal, and the response of endothelial cells to shear stress converts it into decisions about vessel tone, cell shape and inflammation. Steady high-volume laminar flow is atheroprotective: it elongates and aligns cells along the flow axis and activates AKT1 through ligand-independent VEGFR2, nucleotide-sensing P2RY2 and adrenomedullin receptor signalling, which phosphorylates eNOS to raise nitric oxide output and dilate the vessel. Disturbed or low flow instead engages integrin alpha5:beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP hydrolysis and PP2A-dependent dephosphorylation of YAP1, with focal adhesion kinase driving NF-kB activation and a pro-inflammatory transcriptional programme. All flow types open the mechanosensitive channel PIEZO1; the resulting calcium entry activates calpain-2, which cleaves junctional and cytoskeletal substrates near the membrane to remodel morphology. This mechanotransduction underlies the regional susceptibility of arteries to atherosclerosis.

Maple syrup urine disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, the mitochondrial machine performing the second, committed step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism. Without it, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate in blood and urine, producing the characteristic sweet odour along with poor feeding, lethargy, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death in the classic neonatal form; milder intermediate and stress-triggered intermittent forms reflect higher residual activity. The complex is built from an E1 decarboxylase made of BCKDHA and BCKDHB dimers, a DBT transacylase core, and the shared DLD dehydrogenase, and requires thiamine diphosphate, lipoamide, FAD and NAD+. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation, with the phosphatase PPM1K activating the complex. Because DLD also serves pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, its loss causes broader, lethal lactic acidosis. Newborn screening enables dietary intervention.

Building the NuRD complex brings two activities together on the same chromatin remodeler: ATP-dependent nucleosome sliding and histone deacetylation. Assembly is thought to nucleate on a core of HDAC1 or HDAC2 with an MTA paralogue (MTA1, MTA2 or MTA3) and the histone-binding proteins RBBP4/RBBP7, onto which GATAD2A/B, MBD2 or MBD3, CDK2AP1/2 and one of the CHD3, CHD4 or CHD5 ATPases are recruited. Because each subunit position can be filled by a member of a paralogous family, cells make compositionally distinct complexes with overlapping but separable roles, and no complete structure of the assembled complex exists. Recruitment to particular genes depends largely on transcription factors, including Ikaros family zinc fingers and nuclear receptors, rather than on intrinsic DNA or histone binding alone. Once bound, NuRD can repress transcription or activate it, positioning this assembly step upstream of chromatin-based control of gene expression.
